intro: Donald Betts plays “Von fremden Ländern und Menschen” (“Of Foreign Lands and Peoples”), the first piece of Kinderszenen, Op. 15. The tune is in G major, and triplets run between the melody and the bass.

sections.label: A · Tune over triplets
sections.mNote: Eight bars in G major, repeated.

sections.label: B · Paired notes, then a pause
A′ · the G-major tune returns
sections.mNote: The melody begins on D this time.

sections.label: B · Second strain, repeated
sections.mNote: The second strain repeats, with the return of the opening tune.

cues.title: Opening melody over triplets
cues.text: The melody leaps from B to G and comes down F♯–E–D. Under it, triplets pass between the hands while the bass moves in two beats to the bar.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 3, bars 1–8. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Repeat of the opening eight bars
cues.text: The opening eight bars are repeated. The melody again reaches the high G. Beneath it, a B♭ appears in the triplet accompaniment of bars 1 and 3 before the harmony returns to G major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3: repeat after bar 8; B♭ in the triplet accompaniment of bars 1 and 3.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Autograph for Marie Wieck, 1847
cues.text: In 1847 Schumann gave the manuscript of this piece to his sister-in-law Marie Wieck. It is now in the Robert-Schumann-Haus in Zwickau and is the only complete autograph of any of the thirteen Kinderszenen.
cues.evidence: Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (Robert-Schumann-Haus Zwickau, 2013), item 5, autograph 3702–A1. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: Second voice in the right hand
transitions.to: B · Paired notes, then a pause
transitions.how: The phrase ends in G major and the music moves to E minor. At bar 9 the right hand plays in pairs of notes, starting on G and B, over an E–B–E accompaniment, and the triplets continue underneath. The two-beat pulse stays the same, and the new phrase is marked piano.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3, bars 8–10; E–B–E accompaniment under G and B at bar 9.

transitions.title: Fermata before the G-major tune
transitions.from: B · Paired notes, then a pause
transitions.how: The new phrase ends with a ritardando and a fermata. The triplets then resume beneath the G-major tune, marked piano. The tune starts on D, and the leap to G and the descending phrase after it are heard again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3, bars 13–16; melody checked against Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription, based on Leichte Stücke (1900).

transitions.title: Repeat back to the paired notes
transitions.how: The G-major cadence ends on a long B in the melody. At bar 22 the repeat sends the pianist straight back to bar 9, where the paired G and B return over the E-minor accompaniment. The six-bar excursion and the fermata are played again, followed once more by the return.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 3, repeat from bar 22 to bar 9.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The sources do not say which printed edition Donald Betts played from. Schumann’s Kinderszenen exist in a pre-publication printing, the 1839 first edition and its revised second issue, and Clara Schumann’s later edition; the recording is not matched to any of them here.

composer.epithet: A bookseller’s son, composer of piano music depicting lovers, masks and arguments, and a music critic.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
